71.title: The messenger in the eastern place
71.word: The messenger in the eastern pla
71.hook: Maryam withdraws to a quiet place, and a messenger in the form of a man brings impossible news
71.howItsDone: Muslims read this scene in Surah Maryam and Surah Al 'Imran and honor Maryam as a woman of faith and purity; the phrase kun fa-yakun is often said when speaking of what only Allah can do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old man's whisper in the room of prayer, and a son named Yahya. Your line was he called in secret. Did you ask for something quietly? Day seventy-one.

Maryam is grown now. The Qur'an says she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east, and put a screen between herself and them. A place to be alone. Maybe to pray, maybe just to be quiet. The text doesn't say why, and it doesn't need to. And then, in that private place, she isn't alone. A man is standing there. Think about how that would feel for a young woman who has deliberately gone somewhere nobody should be. Her first words are not a scream. They're a name of God. She says: I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you fear Him at all.
screen: `A PLACE TOWARD THE EAST.` → `A SCREEN, AND THEN A MAN.` → `I SEEK REFUGE IN THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells us who he is before she knows: Allah sent Our Spirit to her, and he took the form of a man, well made. Muslims understand the Spirit here as the angel Jibril, the same messenger who, as this path will tell later, came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in a cave. Notice her first move. Before anything else, she reaches for ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, the name inside the bismillah, from day two of this path. And he answers gently: I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son. And then Maryam asks the most honest question in the story. In Pickthall's translation: “How can I have a son when no mortal hath touched me, neither have I been unchaste?” She doesn't pretend to understand. She doesn't say yes to what makes no sense. She asks. And the Qur'an doesn't scold her for asking. The answer is the same one Zakariyya heard yesterday, word for word, for his impossible child: Thy Lord saith, “It is easy for Me.” Easy. Not for Maryam. It will be the hardest thing in her life. Easy for Him. In Surah Al 'Imran the same scene gives the reason: when Allah decides a thing, He only says to it, “Be! and it is.” In Arabic, kun fa-yakun. Christians know this scene too. They call it the Annunciation, and in the Gospel of Luke the angel is Gabriel. Muslims and Christians tell it differently in important ways, and both honor Maryam's courage in that room. What the Qur'an gives today is a young woman alone with a question no human could answer, and an answer that doesn't explain. It just says who is able.
screen: `OUR SPIRIT, IN THE FORM OF A MAN.` · `HOW CAN I HAVE A SON?` · `IT IS EASY FOR ME.` · `KUN FA-YAKUN: BE, AND IT IS.` · then, large: `IT IS EASY FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a question that has no human answer. Settle, and breathe. Let one come. Why this happened. What's next. How something impossible could ever work out. Don't try to answer it. Don't push it away. Just ask it honestly, the way Maryam did, and then sit next to it. If you pray, you can hand it to Allah with her words: I seek refuge in the Most Merciful. If you don't, just let the question stay open. The bell holds the time.
The messenger in the eastern place. Jibril comes to Maryam in a quiet room with news of a son, and to her honest question, the answer is: it is easy for Me.
screen: `THE MESSENGER IN THE EASTERN PLACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it is easy for him. Today, when something looks impossible, ask your honest question out loud, then say the line once. Tomorrow, a palm tree in the desert. Day seventy-one.

72.title: The palm tree
72.hook: alone and in labor, Maryam holds on to a palm trunk, and is told to shake it, eat and drink
72.carry: shake the tree; eat; be glad
72.howItsDone: Muslims read the birth of Isa in Surah Maryam, and many honor the palm tree scene by breaking the Ramadan fast with dates, as the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have done.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jibril in the eastern place, and Maryam's honest question: how? The answer was your line, it is easy for Him. What looked impossible to you? Day seventy-two.

The Qur'an doesn't give us a crowd, or an inn, or a star. It gives us one young woman, far from home. She has gone off to a distant place, alone, and the labor pains begin. They drive her, the Qur'an says, to the trunk of a palm tree, and she holds on to it. Anyone who has been near a birth knows that moment: the pain that comes in waves, the grabbing for anything solid. And in that moment, Maryam, the woman honored above the women of the worlds, says something the Qur'an doesn't hide. She says she wishes she were dead.
screen: `FAR FROM HOME, ALONE.` → `SHE HOLDS THE PALM TRUNK.` → `SHE WISHES SHE WERE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are her words, in Pickthall's translation: “Oh, would that I had died ere this and had become a thing of naught, forgotten!” The Qur'an keeps that line. It lets one of the holiest women in its pages say the worst thing a person in pain can say, and it doesn't correct her. Then a voice calls to her from below. Commentators differ on who: some say the angel Jibril, some say the newborn child himself. And the first thing the voice says is: grieve not. Your Lord has put a stream beneath you. Then comes the part people remember: “And shake the trunk of the palm-tree toward thee, thou wilt cause ripe dates to fall upon thee.” Now, think about it. A woman who has just given birth can't shake a palm trunk. A palm trunk hardly moves even for a strong man. And Muslims have often noticed that. The dates could have simply fallen. Instead she is asked to put her hand on the tree and do her small part, and Allah does the rest. Then, three plain instructions: “So eat and drink and be consoled.” Eat. Drink. Be glad, or cool your eyes, as the Arabic puts it: let your eyes be at rest. Not a sermon. Food, water and comfort for a woman who has just been through labor. Christians tell Jesus's birth in their own way, in Bethlehem with a manger. The Qur'an's picture is this one: a palm tree, a stream and fresh dates. It's one reason dates matter so much to many Muslims, and why many break the Ramadan fast with one.
screen: `WOULD THAT I HAD DIED ERE THIS.` · `GRIEVE NOT: A STREAM BENEATH YOU.` · `SHAKE THE TRUNK; THE DATES FALL.` · `EAT AND DRINK AND BE CONSOLED.` · then, large: `DO YOUR SMALL PART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: if you have one nearby, take a date, or any piece of fruit, and eat it slowly. Look at it first. Notice the color, the weight in your hand. Take one small bite and let it sit on your tongue before you chew. Notice the sweetness arrive. Think of Maryam under the tree, exhausted, being told: eat, drink, be glad. If you pray, you can say bismillah before the first bite and alhamdulillah after the last. The bell holds the time.
The palm tree. In labor and alone, Maryam holds its trunk, shakes it, and fresh dates fall. An-nakhlah, in Arabic.

Your line: shake the tree; eat; be glad. Today, when you're worn out, do one small part, then let yourself eat, drink and rest without guilt. Tomorrow, Maryam goes home with the baby. Day seventy-two.

73.title: The baby who spoke
73.hook: Maryam carries her baby home, says nothing to the accusations, and points to the cradle
73.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Isa speaking in the cradle in Surah Maryam, and many recite his words, peace on me the day I was born, as a blessing on birth, death and rising.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the palm tree: Maryam in labor, a stream beneath her, dates falling. Your line was shake the tree; eat; be glad. Did you let yourself rest? Day seventy-three.

Think of the walk home. Maryam, unmarried, carrying a newborn, heading back toward the people who know her family. There's no way to explain this. Any explanation she gives will sound like an excuse. And she has been told, under the palm tree, what to do: if you meet anyone, say, I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, and I will not speak to anyone today. A fast of silence. So she walks into town, into the stares, and the voices start. O Maryam, you've done a terrible thing. Your father was a good man. Your mother was a decent woman. And Maryam says nothing at all. She just points at the baby.
screen: `CARRYING HIM HOME.` → `A FAST OF SILENCE.` → `SHE POINTS AT THE BABY.`

segments.voice: They're baffled. In Pickthall's words: “How can we talk to one who is in the cradle, a young boy?” And then the baby speaks. “Lo! I am the slave of Allah. He hath given me the Scripture and hath appointed me a Prophet.” His first words are not about himself as a wonder. They're about who he serves: I am a servant of Allah. He goes on: Allah has made me blessed wherever I am, told me to pray and give charity as long as I live, and to be kind to my mother. Not arrogant, not wretched. And then this line, which many Muslims know by heart: “Peace on me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I shall be raised alive!” If that sounds familiar, it should. A few verses earlier, the Qur'an says almost the same words about Yahya, the son of Zakariyya's quiet prayer: peace on him the day he was born, the day he dies, the day he is raised alive. Two cousins, two impossible births, one blessing. Notice who does the defending in this story. Maryam doesn't argue. She doesn't prove anything. She keeps her silence, and the truth speaks for her, from the cradle. One more detail scholars discuss: the crowd calls her sister of Harun, of Aaron. Muslims understand this as a family or priestly connection, or a brother named Harun, not a claim that she was Musa's sister; a hadith in Sahih Muslim says people used to be named after earlier prophets and good people. Muslims count this as the first miracle of Isa: speaking as a baby, to clear his mother's name.
screen: `HOW CAN WE TALK TO A BABY?` · `I AM THE SLAVE OF ALLAH.` · `PEACE ON ME THE DAY I WAS BORN.` · `SHE KEEPS SILENT; THE TRUTH SPEAKS.` · then, large: `LET THE TRUTH SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silent where you'd normally defend yourself. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you've been misunderstood, a comment at work, a family story told wrong, an old accusation. Notice the speech you've been rehearsing. The comeback. The proof. Now, just for this sitting, set it down. Don't argue with anyone in your head. Let it be quiet. If you pray, you can leave your defense with Allah, as Maryam did. The bell holds the time.
The baby who spoke. Maryam keeps her vow of silence, and the child Isa speaks from the cradle: I am a servant of Allah.
Your line: let the truth speak. Once today, when you want to over-explain yourself, say less, and let what's true show on its own. Tomorrow, who Isa is for Muslims. Day seventy-three.

74.title: Isa, prophet of Allah
74.hook: Muslims honor Isa, son of Maryam, as a great prophet and messenger who healed by Allah's leave
74.tomorrow: the one who left in anger
74.howItsDone: Muslims honor Isa as one of the greatest prophets, say 'peace be upon him' after his name, and read his story in Surahs Al 'Imran, Al-Ma'idah and Maryam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baby who spoke from the cradle, and his mother's silence. Your line was let the truth speak. Did you say a little less? Day seventy-four.

Here's something that surprises a lot of people, Muslim and not. Jesus is in the Qur'an. Not in a footnote. His name, Isa, appears around twenty-five times, more often than the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is named. His mother has a surah named after her. His birth, his first words and his miracles are all told. When many Muslims say his name, they add, peace be upon him, the same honor they give every prophet. So after three days in the story of his birth, today steps back and asks: who is Isa, for Muslims?
screen: `JESUS IS IN THE QUR'AN.` → `ABOUT TWENTY-FIVE TIMES.` → `WHO IS ISA, FOR MUSLIMS?`

segments.voice: The Qur'an gives him titles. He is al-Masih, the Messiah. He is called a word from Allah, and a spirit from Him. He was given a scripture, the Injil, the Gospel. And he is counted among the greatest messengers, alongside Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad. Then there are his miracles. In Surah Al 'Imran, Isa speaks to his people and lists them: he shapes a bird from clay and breathes into it, and it becomes a bird. And then, in Pickthall's translation: “I heal him who was born blind, and the leper, and I raise the dead, by Allah's leave.” Listen for that last phrase, because it keeps coming back. By Allah's leave. By Allah's permission. In Arabic, bi-idhni llah. It appears again and again when the Qur'an describes what Isa did. The miracles are real, the Qur'an says, and they are Allah's. Isa is the one they come through. That phrase holds the heart of how Muslims see him: a great and beloved prophet, born of a virgin mother, a healer, and a servant of Allah, not Allah himself. Here the two neighboring faiths part ways, and it's worth saying plainly who believes what. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, that he died on the cross and rose again. Muslims honor him as a prophet and messenger, and the Qur'an says he was not killed or crucified, though it was made to appear so, and that Allah raised him up. Many Muslims believe he will return before the end. Both faiths love him. They understand him differently, and each holds its understanding with deep seriousness.
screen: `AL-MASIH: A WORD AND A SPIRIT.` · `THE BIRD OF CLAY, THE BLIND, THE DEAD.` · `BI-IDHNI LLAH: BY ALLAH'S LEAVE.` · `TWO FAITHS, TWO UNDERSTANDINGS.` · then, large: `A SERVANT OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer healing words to someone who's unwell. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who is sick, or hurting, or worn down right now. Picture them clearly. What would help them hear? Not advice. Something kind. I'm thinking of you. You're not alone. I'll bring dinner Thursday. Choose the words. If you pray, you can ask Allah to heal them, since the healing is His. Then, when the bell ends, send those words. The bell holds the time.
Isa. Jesus, son of Maryam: in Islam, the Messiah, a great prophet and messenger, who healed by Allah's leave.

Your line: by Allah's leave. Today, when something you do goes well, remember it came through you, not only from you. That closes Maryam and Isa: a vow, a whisper, a messenger, a palm tree, a cradle, a healer. Tomorrow, a man who left in anger. Day seventy-four.

75.title: The one who left in anger
75.word: The one who left in anger
75.hook: Yunus gives up on his people, walks off in anger, boards a crowded ship, and is thrown into the sea
75.carry: walking away is also a choice
75.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Yunus in Surahs Yunus, Al-Anbiya, As-Saffat and Al-Qalam, and honor him as a prophet whose story teaches patience with people and turning back to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isa, the Messiah and healer, who did it all by Allah's leave. That was your line. Did something good come through you? Today, a new prophet and a very different mood. Day seventy-five.

You know the feeling. You've explained it ten times. You've been patient. You've tried everything. And they still won't listen. So you grab your keys, you don't slam the door but you close it hard, and you go. That's where this story starts. A prophet named Yunus has been calling his people to Allah, and they won't have it. And the Qur'an says, simply, he went off in anger. He walks down to the harbor, finds a ship loaded to the rails with cargo and passengers, and gets on board. Anywhere but here. Then, out at sea, the weather turns.
screen: `THEY WON'T LISTEN.` → `HE WENT OFF IN ANGER.` → `A SHIP LOADED TO THE RAILS.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells this story in pieces, in several surahs. In Surah Al-Anbiya it gives him a nickname, in Pickthall's words: “And (mention) Dhu'n-Nun, when he went off in anger.” Dhu n-Nun: the one of the fish. In Surah As-Saffat, the ship: “When he fled unto the laden ship.” Fled. The Arabic word used here is the one for a runaway slave leaving his master. That's how the text names what he did. Commentators explain that Yunus left his people before Allah had given him leave to go. His frustration was understandable. His leaving was still a choice. Then the storm. The ship is overloaded and in danger, and the sailors decide someone has to go over the side. They cast lots, and the lot falls on Yunus. He's thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallows him. The Qur'an says he was blameworthy at that moment. It doesn't pretend otherwise. And yet here's what's striking. Yunus is still a prophet, honored by name. The tenth surah is called Yunus. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have said that no one should say he is better than Yunus, son of Matta. The one who walked out is not written off. Another surah even tells the Prophet: be patient, and don't be like the companion of the fish. The lesson is gentle: Yunus is a warning and a beloved prophet at once. Jews and Christians know him too, as Jonah, from the Hebrew Bible. For now, leave him where the Qur'an leaves him today: in the dark, inside the fish.
screen: `DHU N-NUN: THE ONE OF THE FISH.` · `HE FLED UNTO THE LADEN SHIP.` · `THE LOTS FALL ON YUNUS.` · `NO ONE IS BETTER THAN YUNUS.` · then, large: `WALKING AWAY IS ALSO A CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you walked out angry. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place, a person, a job, a conversation, where you left in frustration. Maybe you were right to be frustrated. Don't argue that. Just notice the moment of leaving. What did it feel like in your body? What did you tell yourself as you went? Was it a choice, or did it feel like the only option? If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you what you couldn't see then. The bell holds the time.
The one who left in anger. Yunus, Dhu n-Nun, walks away from his people before he's told to, and ends up in the sea.
screen: `THE ONE WHO LEFT IN ANGER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: walking away is also a choice. Today, if you feel the urge to walk out of something, stop for one breath and ask: am I choosing this, or just fleeing? Tomorrow, what Yunus says in the dark. Day seventy-five.

76.title: Three darknesses
76.hook: in the night, in the sea, inside the fish, Yunus calls out: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong
76.tomorrow: the gourd and the saved city
76.howItsDone: Many Muslims say the prayer of Yunus, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina z-zalimin, in times of distress, sometimes repeating it many times, trusting the hadith that it is answered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunus left his people in anger and ended up in the sea. Your line was walking away is also a choice. Did you catch yourself about to flee? Day seventy-six.

Have you ever been somewhere truly dark? Not a room with the lights off. The kind of dark where you hold your hand in front of your face and there's nothing. Now stack it. It's night. Under the night, the sea. Under the sea, inside a great fish, a man. Early commentators called it three darknesses: the dark of the night, the dark of the water, the dark of the belly of the fish. No ship. No crew. No one who could possibly hear him. And the man who walked out on his people in anger now has nowhere left to walk. And in there, he says something.
screen: `THE DARK OF THE NIGHT.` → `THE DARK OF THE SEA.` → `THE DARK OF THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Anbiya says he cried out in the darkness. And here is his prayer, in Pickthall's translation: “There is no God save Thee. Be Thou glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer.” In Arabic: la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina z-zalimin. Three short pieces. Look at each one. First, la ilaha illa anta: there is no god but You. That's tawhid, day ten of this path, but said face to face. Not about Allah, to Him. Second, subhanaka: glory to You. You are beyond all this, above any fault. Third, and hardest: I was one of the wrongdoers. No excuse. No mention of how stubborn his people were. He doesn't say, they drove me to it. He says, I was wrong. You've heard that shape before on this path. Adam and Hawwa: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. Musa after the blow: my Lord, I have wronged myself. The prophets keep saying it. And then the next verse: “Then we heard his prayer and saved him from the anguish. Thus we save believers.” Notice that last line. Thus we save believers. Not just Yunus. The Qur'an turns the story outward. And a hadith in Tirmidhi says that the prayer of Dhu n-Nun, whenever a Muslim calls with it for anything, is answered. Which is why so many Muslims know these words by heart, and say them in their own dark places: in a hospital corridor, in debt, at three in the morning. Another surah adds that if Yunus had not been one who glorified Allah, he would have stayed in the belly of the fish until the day of rising.
screen: `LA ILAHA ILLA ANTA: NO GOD BUT YOU.` · `SUBHANAKA: GLORY TO YOU.` · `I HAVE BEEN A WRONG-DOER.` · `WE HEARD HIS PRAYER AND SAVED HIM.` · then, large: `THUS WE SAVE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Close your eyes and let it be dark. If you pray, say the prayer of Yunus slowly, three times, silently or in a whisper: la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina z-zalimin. There is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. Leave a breath between each piece. If you don't pray, simply listen to the words in your mind, and let the last one land: I was wrong. Notice what it's like to say it without an excuse. The bell holds the time.
Three darknesses. The night, the sea and the fish, where Yunus called: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong.

Your line: la ilaha illa anta. There is no god but You. Today, when you find yourself in a dark moment, say it once, or just remember that Yunus did. Tomorrow, what happened when he came out. Day seventy-six.

77.title: The gourd and the saved city
77.word: The gourd and the saved city
77.hook: Yunus is cast ashore, sick, and shaded by a gourd vine, and the people he walked away from turn back and are spared
77.tomorrow: Mecca, a valley of trade and idols
77.howItsDone: Muslims read the end of Yunus's story in Surah As-Saffat and Surah Yunus, and it is often recalled as a reminder that no one should despair of a people turning back to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three darknesses, and Yunus's prayer from inside the fish. Your line was la ilaha illa anta: there is no god but You. Did you say it anywhere dark? Day seventy-seven, the end of week eleven.

Picture a beach, empty and bare, under a hard sun. The fish opens its mouth and a man tumbles out onto the sand. Weak. Sick. His skin raw from the inside of the fish. He can barely lift his head. He has nothing. No shade, no food, no one. The Qur'an says Allah cast him on a bare shore while he was sick. And then, right over him, something begins to grow. A vine, with wide green leaves, spreading over his body like an umbrella. The Qur'an names the plant. It's a gourd.
screen: `A BARE SHORE, A SICK MAN.` → `NO SHADE, NO ONE.` → `A VINE BEGINS TO GROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the line in Pickthall's translation: “And We caused a tree of gourd to grow above him.” In Arabic, yaqtin. Commentators explain it as a fast-growing gourd with broad leaves, the kind that gives quick shade and keeps flies away from a sick man's skin. A small mercy, exactly sized to what he needed. Then the Qur'an turns to the part of the story Yunus never saw coming: “And We sent him to a hundred thousand (folk) or more.” And they believed. The people he walked out on. The ones he was sure would never listen. They turned back to Allah. Surah Yunus, the tenth surah, the one named for him, makes something remarkable of this. It says there was no other town among the ones warned of old that believed in time and was spared, except the people of Yunus. When they believed, the punishment was lifted from them, and they were given enjoyment of life for a while. Think about the shape of it. Yunus left because he was certain they wouldn't change. And they changed. His anger was sure, and it was wrong. Commentators say the people went out together, men, women and children, and cried to Allah when they saw the warning signs, and they were spared. This is the only whole city in the Qur'an's stories of the prophets that turned around in time. And that closes week eleven: a messenger in the eastern place, a palm tree, a baby who spoke, Isa by Allah's leave, a man who left in anger, three darknesses, and a gourd vine over a city that believed.
screen: `A TREE OF GOURD ABOVE HIM.` · `A HUNDRED THOUSAND OR MORE.` · `THE ONLY TOWN SPARED IN TIME.` · `HIS ANGER WAS SURE, AND WRONG.` · then, large: `THE CITY BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back to one thing you left. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you walked away from, or someone you gave up on, a friendship, a project, a skill, a relative. Maybe you were sure it would never change. Just picture it now, today, without the old certainty. What if it has changed? What if you have? Choose one small step back toward it: a text, an email, ten minutes. If you pray, you can ask Allah to open the way. The bell holds the time.
The gourd and the saved city. A vine shades a sick prophet on the shore, and the people he gave up on turn back and are spared.
screen: `THE GOURD AND THE SAVED CITY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the city believed. Today, take the one small step back toward what you left. Eleven weeks on the path. Tomorrow, the stories of the prophets arrive in a valley called Mecca. Day seventy-seven.
